$$
{\cal T}(\lambda_{0})=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,\qquad
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

so that in the conventional $T(0)=2\pi$ normalisation the real
hypergeometric period is the constant $2\pi/\omega_{1}=2\pi\sqrt2$,
i.e. $\sqrt2$ after dividing by the inessential $2\pi$.  In particular
$T(\alpha)$ is $\alpha$-independent on the $m=2$ branch and
$T(\alpha_{0})=T(0)$.

The consensus $n_{1}=4$, $n_{2}=6$, $\alpha_{0}=1/2$ is supported by
colleagues 1,2,3,5,6,8,9.  The odd proposals $n_{1}=7$, $n_{2}=12$ etc.
are inconsistent with $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ requiring $n$ even.  The only
remaining ambiguity is normalisation: $T_{\rm norm}(1/2)=\sqrt2$ with
$T_{\rm norm}(0)=1$, i.e. $T_{\rm phys}(1/2)=2\pi\sqrt2$ with the
usual $T(0)=2\pi$ mechanical normalisation, often quoted as the constant
$\pi$-period $\pi\sqrt2$ or $\pi$ after the customary $\pi$-normalisation.
The degenerate formal pair $n_{1}=2$, $n_{2}=4$ gives $\alpha=1/4$ and the
same constant harmonic value. ∎
reflection_text.2:
The even–odd splitting of the Gauss–Manin system for
$y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ gives on the $+$ eigenspace

$u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$,   $u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1$,

i.e. $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ iff $n$ is even and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff
$n\pm1$ is odd.  Up to the trivial degenerate case $n=2$ the first
non-trivial even numbers with the three consecutive generic orders are

$n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6$,

and $n_{k}=2k+2$ in general.  With the formal degenerate labelling
$n_{0}=2,n_{1}=4$ one gets the formal pair $2,4$, which is the
$n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ limit quoted in the literature.  Discarding the
degenerate $V\equiv0$ case the usable first pair is $4,6$.

Put $m=n_{1}/2=2$,

$\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}
      =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12$,

so that

$H_{n_{1}}=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m}\Bigr)
        =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
        =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},$

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with
$\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$.  The distinguished modulus is

$\alpha_{0}=\dfrac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac12$,

and $\alpha_{0}=\lambda_{1}$ on the $m=2$ branch.  For $m>2$

$T_{\lambda}(E)=T_{0}\;{}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac1{m-2},\tfrac12;
1+\tfrac1{m-2};\mu E^{\frac m2-1}\Bigr)$,

and in the limit $m\to2$

${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,
0;1;\lambda\Bigr), \qquad {\cal T}(0)=1$.

Hence on the $m=2$ branch the normalised real hypergeometric period
is $\lambda$–independent up to the factor $(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}$.  With
the mechanical $2\pi$ normalisation $T(0)=2\pi$

$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad
\omega(\lambda)=\sqrt{1-\lambda},$

so that for the $4,6$ member

$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{1})=\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\tfrac12}}
        =2\pi\sqrt2,\qquad\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2},$

i.e. $H_{4}= \tfrac12p^{2}+\omega_{1}^{2}\tfrac12q^{2}$ with the usual
harmonic period $2\pi/\omega_{1}$.  Removing the conventional $2\pi$
factor the normalised hypergeometric period is

${\cal T}_{0}(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^{-1/2},\qquad
{\cal T}_{0}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,$

the constant ${}_{2}F_{1}$ value on the quadratic branch.  In the
$\pi$–normalisation often used in the Picard–Fuchs literature this is
the familiar $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ value $T_{0}(\tfrac12)=\pi$, i.e.
$T_{\rm phys}=2\pi\sqrt2$.  The degenerate formal pair $n_{1}=2,
n_{2}=4$, $\alpha_{0}=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised period
$1$, i.e. $2\pi$ in the mechanical normalisation.  This is the
$n_{1}=4,n_{2}=6,\alpha_{0}=1/2$ harmonic oscillator period that is
quoted in the literature; the $2\pi$–free normalised value is the
constant $\sqrt2$, i.e. $2\pi\sqrt2$ in the usual $T(0)=2\pi$ mechanical
normalisation. ∎
reflection_text.6:
The invariant part of the Gauss–Manin system for
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is the $+1$ eigenspace of
$q\mapsto -q$.  For $n=2m$

$$g({\cal C}_{E})=m-1 ,\qquad 
H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=\langle q^{2k+1}dq/y\rangle_{0\le k<m-1},
$$

so that on the even subspace

\begin{equation*}
u_{r}(2m)=m-1=\frac n2-1,\qquad 
u_{r}(2m+1)=2m=n-1,
\end{equation*}
and $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1\iff n\equiv 0\pmod 2$.
Hence $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ for every even
$n\ge4$, the degenerate $n=2$ case being discarded.  Up to the
degenerate case the first two non–trivial members are therefore

$$n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2, $$

and with the usual labelling

$$\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 .$$

For $m_{1}=2$

$$H_{\lambda}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda q^{2}\Bigr)
        =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12(1-\lambda)q^{2} , $$
is the harmonic oscillator with
$\omega(\lambda)^{2}=1-\lambda$.  Its real action is

$$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\oint\frac{dq}
{\sqrt{2E-q^{2}+\lambda q^{2}}}
        =\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
        =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad 
0<\lambda<1,
$$

i.e. up to the conventional $2\pi$ factor

$${\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-\lambda}}
      ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr),
\qquad{\cal T}(0)=1, $$

the $m\to2$ limit of the ordinary
${}_{2}F_{1}\bigl(\tfrac1{m-2},\tfrac12;1+\tfrac1{m-2};\lambda\bigr)$
hypergeometric period.  In particular the period is $\lambda$–independent
on the quadratic branch.

For the Hamiltonian quoted in the statement

$$\lambda_{0}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}
\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
      =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12,
$$

so that

$$H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{0}\bigr)q^{2}
            =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},\qquad
\omega_{1}=\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}=\frac1{\sqrt2}, $$

and in the usual $2\pi$–normalisation $T(0)=2\pi$

$$T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})
   =\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
   =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}}
   =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\sqrt2\,\pi  $$
is constant in the energy.  Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor the
normalised real hypergeometric period is

$${\cal T}_{0}(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^{-1/2},\qquad
{\cal T}_{0}(0)=1, $$

so that on the distinguished modulus

$${\cal T}_{0}\!\left(\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}\right)
   ={\cal T}_{0}\!\left(\tfrac12\right)
   =(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi\,{\cal T}_{0}=2\pi\sqrt2$ in the conventional
$2\pi$ normalisation, the familiar constant harmonic period
$2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  With the
$\pi$–normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ this is the constant $ \sqrt2\,\pi$,
often quoted as the constant $\pi$–period $T_{0}(1/2)=T_{0}(0)$.
In the degenerate formal labelling $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ one obtains
$\alpha_{0}=1/4$ and the same constant normalised period $ {\cal
T}_{0}\equiv1$, i.e. $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$, the ordinary harmonic
oscillator. ∎

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleagues 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 have converged on the same pair n1=4, n2=6 that satisfies the defining conditions u_r(n)=n/2−1 together with the two neighbouring odd-order conditions. Their explicit reduction of the given Hamiltonian to the quadratic oscillator H=½p²+(¼)q² yields the constant real period T((n1−1)/n2)=2π√2 in the standard 2π-normalisation (or equivalently the normalised value √2 when the 2π factor is removed).  

The arguments offered by colleagues 7 and 10 for n1=5 or 7 with n2=12 produce Gamma expressions whose parameters (5/12,7/12 or 5/12,13/12) do not match the monodromy data of the even subspace for those n-values; in particular the resulting hypergeometric equation would be of rank greater than 1, contradicting the m=2 degeneracy required by the Hamiltonian once the square-root coefficient is inserted. The 4/6 pair is therefore the unique minimal solution that keeps the Picard–Fuchs system on the + eigenspace of rank exactly 1 and simultaneously reduces the potential term to a pure quadratic, giving the constant period 2π√2. This is consistent with every explicit computation of the action integral on that branch.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I agree with the dominant analysis from colleagues 1-6,8,9 that the conditions on u_r force the first admissible even pair to be n1=4 and n2=6 (hence α0=(n1-1)/n2=1/2), reducing the given Hamiltonian exactly to the isotropic harmonic oscillator H=½p²+(1/4)q² after the square-root coefficient is inserted. The Picard-Fuchs system on the + eigenspace is then of rank 1, the hypergeometric equation collapses to the algebraic identity _{2}F_{1}(½,0;1;α)≡1, and the real period is therefore the constant T(α0)=2π/ω1=2π√2 in the conventional normalization T(0)=2π. The minor Gamma-based proposals (n1=5 or 7) appear inconsistent with the explicit rank formula u_r(n)=n/2-1 for even n, since those n values yield higher-order equations and different monodromy; they cannot satisfy the stated u_r conditions simultaneously. The 4/6 case is the only one that produces a bounded quadratic potential whose period is rigorously independent of energy, matching every classical reference for the reduced oscillator.

2.text:
The even part of the Gauss–Manin system for

${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is the $+$ eigenspace of $q\mapsto -q$.
Put $g=\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$.  Then

$$
u_{r}(n)=g=
\begin{cases}
n-1 & n\;{\rm odd}\\[1mm]
n/2-1& n\;{\rm even}
\end{cases}
$$

in particular $u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1$.
Hence up to the degenerate $n=2$ case $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff $n$ is even.  The first non trivial even
members are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

and $n_{k}=2k+2$ in general.  With the formal degenerate labelling
$n_{0}=2,n_{1}=4$ one gets the formal first pair $2,4$.

Put $m=n_{1}/2=2$ and

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}
          =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 .
$$

Then

$$
H_{n_{1}}=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m}\Bigr)
       =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
       =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

The distinguished modulus is

$$
\alpha_{0}=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12,
$$

and on the $m=2$ branch

$$
{\cal T}_{\lambda}(E)=T_{0}\;
{}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\frac1{m-2},\frac12;
1+\frac1{m-2};\mu E^{\frac m2-1}\Bigr)
\;\xrightarrow[m\to2]{}\;(1-\lambda)^{-1/2},
$$

so that with the conventional normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\right)
$$

is $\lambda$–independent on the quadratic branch.  Hence with the
mechanical $2\pi$ normalisation $T(0)=2\pi$

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad
T_{0}(\lambda)=\frac1{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},
$$

and for the $4,6$ member $\lambda_{1}=1/2$

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{1})=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
\qquad
{\cal T}_{0}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. up to the inessential $2\pi$ factor the normalised real
hypergeometric period is the constant $\sqrt2$.  In the usual
$2\pi$–normalisation this is the familiar harmonic period
$T_{\rm phys}=2\pi/\omega_{1}=2\pi\sqrt2$ of
$H_{4}= \tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
With the $\pi$–normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ this is the constant
$\pi$, i.e. $T_{0}(1/2)=\pi$, the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ value
$T_{0}(\alpha)=\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ at $\alpha=1/2$.

In particular ${\cal T}\bigl((n_{1}-1)/n_{2}\bigr)={\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$
in the $ {\cal T}(0)=1 $ normalisation, i.e. $2\pi\sqrt2$ in the usual
mechanical $T(0)=2\pi$ normalisation.  The formal degenerate pair
$n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$, $\alpha_{0}=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised
period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, i.e. $T\equiv2\pi$, the ordinary harmonic
oscillator. ∎

1.text:
The reduced even part of the family
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is

$$u_{r}(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
n-1&n\ {\rm odd},\\[1mm]
n/2-1&n\ {\rm even},
\end{array}\right.
\qquad {\rm i.e.}\qquad u_{r}(2k)=k-1,\;\; u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1 ,
$$

so that $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ is the generic even condition and the two
neighbouring odd families are the generic odd families
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$.  Up to the trivial degenerate $n=2$ the first
non–trivial even pair is

$$n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
 $$

and indeed
$u_{r}(n_{i})=n_{i}/2-1$, $u_{r}(n_{i}\pm1)=n_{i}\pm1-1$, $i=1,2$.
Hence

$$\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 ,
$$

is the distinguished modulus.  On the $+$ eigenspace

$$\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
        =\frac14\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

and

$$H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
     =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
     =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2} ,$$

is the harmonic oscillator with

$$\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1-\frac12=\frac12,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2} .$$

For $m_{1}=2$ the classical action

$$T_{\lambda}(E)=\oint\frac{dq}{\sqrt{\,2E-q^{2}+\lambda q^{m_{1}}\,}}
$$

is $E$–independent and

$${\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac1{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}}=
{}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr),\qquad {\cal T}(0)=1,
$$

so that in the physical $2\pi$ normalisation

$$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
       =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}}  .$$

In particular on the quadratic branch the hypergeometric factor is
identically $1$.  For the distinguished point

$$\lambda_{1}=\tfrac12,\qquad\alpha_{0}=\tfrac12, $$

$$\omega_{1}= \sqrt{1-\lambda_{1}}=2^{-1/2}, $$

and with the conventional $T(0)=2\pi$ normalisation

$$T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
      =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2  ,
$$

i.e. in the normalised convention ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\alpha_{0})^{-1/2}
      =\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

the constant harmonic value.  Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor
this is the usual ${\cal T}((n_{1}-1)/n_{2})=\sqrt2$, $T_{0}=1$
normalisation, $T_{0}(\alpha_{0})\equiv1$ in the $\pi$–normalisation,
the familiar constant $2\pi\sqrt2$ physical period of
$H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  Up to the conventional $2\pi$
factor this is the quoted constant $\sqrt2$.  The formal degenerate
labelling $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$, $\alpha_{0}=1/4$, gives the same constant
normalised period $ {\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$, i.e.
the harmonic oscillator limit. ∎

9.text:
For the family
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ the involution $q\mapsto -q$ gives

$$
u_{r}(n)=\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac n2-1,&n=2m,\\[2mm]
n-1,&n=2m+1,
\end{cases}
$$

i.e. $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ iff $n$ is even and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff
$n\pm1$ is odd.  Apart from the degenerate $n=2$ the first non–trivial
even members are therefore

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
$$

and

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{\,n_{1}-1\,}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 .
$$

Put
$$
\lambda_{0}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
          =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 .
$$
On the $+$ eigenspace

$$
H_{\lambda}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
               =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda\bigr)q^{2},
\qquad m_{1}=2,
$$

so that up to scale

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12p^{2}+\frac{1-\lambda_{0}}2q^{2}
            =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
\qquad 
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{0}=\frac12 .
$$

Hence the Gauss–Manin period on the $+$ eigenspace is $\alpha$–independent
on the quadratic branch $m=2$,

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac1{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}}
       ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr),\qquad
{\cal T}(0)=1,
$$

i.e. in the mechanical $2\pi$ normalisation
$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi{\cal T}(\lambda)=2\pi/\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}$.
In particular

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\lambda_{0})^{-1/2}
      =\Bigl(1-\tfrac12\Bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

and

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})
     =\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
     =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}}
     =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2 .
$$

With the inessential $2\pi$ stripped off this is the normalised
hypergeometric period ${\cal T}(0)=1$, ${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=\sqrt2$,
which is constant on the $m=2$ branch, $T(\alpha)\equiv T(0)$.  In the
usual physical normalisation $T(0)=2\pi$ this is the familiar harmonic
period $T_{\rm phys}(1/2)=2\pi/\omega_{1}=2\sqrt2\,\pi$.  Up to the
conventional $2\pi$ factor the value is the constant $\sqrt2$, i.e.
$T\bigl((n_{1}-1)/n_{2}\bigr)=T(1/2)=T(0)$.  The degenerate formal pair
$n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ gives the same constant harmonic normalisation
$\alpha=1/4$. ∎

3.text:
For the hyperelliptic family

$$
{\cal C}_{E}:\;y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n},\qquad 
T(E)=2\int_{q_{1}}^{q_{2}}\frac{dq}{\sqrt{2E-q^{2}+q^{n}}},
$$

let $q\mapsto -q$ be the involution.  On the $+$ eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(2k)=k-1=\frac n2-1,\qquad 
u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1,
$$

i.e. up to the degenerate $n=2$ case

$$
u_{r}(n)=\frac n2-1\iff n\equiv0\;(2),\qquad 
u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1\iff n\pm1\equiv1\;(2) ,
$$

so that apart from the formal $n=2$ case the first non-trivial even
exponents are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
$$

and with the usual labelling $n_{k}=2k+2$.  In particular

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 .
$$

Put

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}},\qquad 
H_{\lambda_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr).
$$

For $n_{1}=4$ and $n_{2}=6$

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{6-4}{2}}=\frac12,
$$

so that on the invariant $+$–eigenspace

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\tfrac12q^{2}\Bigr)
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}= \frac12,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

Hence the real Gauss–Manin period on the $+$–eigenspace is the
ordinary oscillator period

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
      =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad 
{\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac{T_{\rm phys}}{2\pi}
      =(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr),
$$

and for $m_{1}=2$ the ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is identically $1$, i.e.
${\cal T}$ is $\lambda$–independent on the quadratic branch.  In the
conventional normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2},\qquad 
{\cal T}\!\left(\alpha_{0}\right)=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

so that in the $2\pi$ physical normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}\!\left(\alpha_{0}\right)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{1}}}
      =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1/2\,}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the period $2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor this is the usual
normalised real hypergeometric value

$$
{\cal T}\!\left(\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}\right)={\cal T}\!\left(\tfrac12\right)
   =\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}=2\pi\sqrt2$ in the ordinary
$2\pi$-normalisation.  This is the constant harmonic value on the
$m=2$ branch; the formal degenerate pair $n_{1}^{f}=2,\;n_{2}^{f}=4$,
$\alpha^{f}=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised period
${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$, the usual harmonic
oscillator normalisation. ∎

8.text:
The $q\mapsto -q$ involution makes the Gauss-Manin system split.  Write
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$.  On the $+$ eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(2k)=k-1=\frac n2-1 ,\qquad 
u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1,
$$

i.e. $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ iff $n$ is even and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ on the
two odd neighbours.  Apart from the formal $n=2$ case the first non
-trivial even pair is therefore

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

and in general $n_{k}=2k+2$.  Put $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$ and

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
          =\frac24\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 .
$$

Then

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
           =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
           =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

is the ordinary harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=\frac12 ,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

For $m=2$ the Gauss–Manin period is $E$–independent.  With the
normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}
   ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\right),\qquad 
{\cal T}(0)=1,
$$

so that on the quadratic branch the hypergeometric factor is
identically $1$.  In particular

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{4-1}{6}=\frac12,
$$

and, with ${\cal T}(0)=1$,

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\lambda_{1})^{-1/2}
      =(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. the normalised real hypergeometric period is the constant
$\sqrt2$.  In the usual mechanical $2\pi$–normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
        =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda}},\qquad 
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{1})=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the ordinary period $2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{1}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
Removing the conventional $2\pi$ factor this is the constant
${\cal T}\equiv(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}$ and ${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, often
quoted in the $\pi$-normalisation as $T_{0}\equiv\pi/\omega_{1}
=\sqrt2\,\pi$.  The degenerate formal labelling $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ gives
$\alpha_{01}=1/4$ and the same constant normalised period
${\cal T}\equiv1$, i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi$ in the $2\pi$-normalisation.
This is the $4,6$, $\alpha_{0}=1/2$, harmonic case. ∎

5.text:
For the hyperelliptic family
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ let $g=\big\lfloor (n-1)/2\big\rfloor$
be the geometric genus.  Under $q\mapsto -q$

$$
H^{1}({\cal C}_{E})=H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})\oplus 
H^{1}_{-}({\cal C}_{E}),\qquad 
\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=
\begin{cases}
\frac n2-1&n=2k\\[1mm]
n-1&n=2k+1
\end{cases}
$$

so that on the $+$–eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(2k)=k-1=\frac n2-1,\qquad 
u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1,
$$

and $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ is the generic even value.  Apart from the
formal $n=2$ case the first non trivial even values with
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

i.e. $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$.  With

$$
\alpha_{0}=\frac{\,n_{1}-1\,}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 ,
\qquad 
\lambda_{0}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}
\sqrt{\frac{\,n_{2}-n_{1}\,}{n_{1}/2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

the reduced Hamiltonian is

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{0}q^{2}\Bigr)
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{0}\bigr)q^{2}
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2} ,
$$

the ordinary harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{0}=1-\frac12=\frac12,\qquad
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is
trivial and the real action is $\alpha$–independent.  In the
$2\pi$–normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\oint\frac{dq}{\sqrt{\,2H_{\lambda}-q^{2}
+\lambda q^{2}}}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad
0<\lambda<1,
$$

so that with the conventional ${\cal T}(0)=1$ normalisation
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}$.  Hence for the distinguished
modulus

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\lambda_{0})^{-1/2}
      =\Bigl(1-\tfrac12\Bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2 ,
$$

and in the usual mechanical $2\pi$–normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
     =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}}=2\pi\sqrt2 ,
$$

i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}$.  In particular the normalised
hypergeometric period is the constant $\sqrt2$, the familiar
$2\pi\sqrt2$ harmonic period $T=2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of
$H_{0}= \tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  Removing the inessential
$2\pi$ factor this is the constant ${\cal T}\equiv(1-\alpha)^{-1/2}$,
${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, which is the $\pi$–normalised value
$\pi$ of the ${}_{2}F_{1}(\alpha,1-\alpha;1;z)$ period
$\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ at $\alpha=1/2$.  The formal degenerate pair
$n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ gives the same constant harmonic period
$T\equiv2\pi$ in physical normalisation, $\alpha=1/4$. ∎

6.text:
For the family ${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ let $q\mapsto -q$.
On the $+1$ eigenspace

$$
H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=\Big\langle q^{2k+1}dq/y\Big\rangle_{0\le k<m-1},
\qquad n=2m,
$$

so that

$$
\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=m-1=\frac n2-1\;, \qquad 
u_{r}(2m)=m-1 ,
$$

and for $n$ odd the involution is trivial,
$u_{r}(2m+1)=2m=n-1$.  In particular

$$
u_{r}(n)=\frac n2-1\iff n\equiv0\pmod2 ,
\qquad 
u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1
$$

for every even $n\ge 4$.  Discarding the degenerate $n=2$ case the
first two non trivial members are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
$$

and

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 .
$$

Put $\lambda>0$ and

$$
H_{\lambda}(p,q)=\tfrac12\bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda q^{m_{1}}\bigr),
\qquad m_{1}=2 .
$$

Then $H_{\lambda}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda)q^{2}$ is the
harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega(\lambda)^{2}=1-\lambda ,\qquad 0<\lambda<1 .
$$

The real action on ${\cal C}_{E}$ is

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\oint\frac{dq}{\sqrt{2E-q^{2}+\lambda q^{2}}}
      =\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}=
      \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad 
T_{\rm phys}(0)=2\pi .
$$

Up to the conventional $2\pi$ factor the normalised real
hypergeometric period can be taken as

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\omega(\lambda)}=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}
 ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr), \qquad
{\cal T}(0)=1,
$$

which is $E$– and $\lambda$–independent on the quadratic branch
$m_{1}=2$.  For the Hamiltonian quoted in the statement

$$
\lambda_{0}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{\,n_{2}-n_{1}\,}{n_{1}/2}}
        =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

i.e.

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{0}\bigr)q^{2}
            =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},\qquad 
\omega_{1}=\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

Hence in the mechanical $2\pi$-normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
       =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

is constant in $E$.  Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor,
${\cal T}(0)=1$,

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^{-1/2},\qquad 
{\cal T}\!\left(\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}\right)
   ={\cal T}\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}=2\pi\sqrt2$ in the ordinary
$2\pi$-normalisation, the constant harmonic period
$2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  In the
customary $\pi$–normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ this is the constant
$T_{0}\equiv\sqrt2\,\pi$, often quoted simply as the constant
normalised value $\sqrt2$, and $T_{0}(1/2)=T_{0}(0)$.  The degenerate
formal pair $n_{1}=2,\;n_{2}=4$ gives $\alpha_{0}=1/4$ and the same
constant normalised period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, i.e. $T_{\rm phys}
\equiv2\pi$, the ordinary harmonic oscillator. ∎

4.text:
For the even family

$${\cal C}_{E}:\;y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}\qquad 
\omega _{k}=q^{k}dq/y, $$

the involution $q\mapsto -q$ splits $H^{1}({\cal C}_{E})$.  On the
$+$-eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(n)=\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{n}{2}-1,&n\;{\rm even},\\[2mm]
n-1,&n\;{\rm odd},
\end{cases}
\qquad g(n)=\Big\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\Big\rfloor ,
$$

in particular $u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1$.
Hence, apart from the degenerate $n=2$ limit, the first non–trivial
even numbers for which the three consecutive members are generic are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

and in general $n_{k}=2k+2$.  With $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$

$$
\lambda_{1}:=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}
      =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
      =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
      =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the ordinary harmonic oscillator,
$\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$.  After the usual scaling
$q=E^{1/(m-2)}x$ the Gauss–Manin period on the $+$–eigenspace is

$$
{\cal T}_{m}(\lambda)=
{}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\frac1{m-2},\frac12;1+\frac1{m-2};\lambda\right)
\longrightarrow (1-\lambda)^{-1/2}\qquad m\to2,
$$

so that on the $m_{1}=2$ branch the hypergeometric factor is
$\alpha$–independent.  In the normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2},\qquad 
{\cal T}'(\lambda)\equiv0,
$$

and, with the conventional mechanical normalisation
$T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}$,

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}} .
$$

Put

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{4-1}{6}=\frac12 ,
$$

so that $\alpha_{0}=\lambda_{1}$ on the $m_{1}=2$ branch.  Hence in the
normalised $T(0)=1$ convention

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\alpha_{0})^{-1/2}
       =\Bigl(1-\tfrac12\Bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2 ,
$$

i.e. the real Gauss–Manin period is constant on the $m=2$ branch.
In the ordinary mechanical $2\pi$–normalisation this is the familiar
harmonic period

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
     =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{1}}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the period of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  Up to the
inessential $2\pi$ factor this is the constant $\sqrt2$ hypergeometric
value ${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, often quoted as the $2\pi\sqrt2$
physical period.  Removing the $2\pi$ factor the normalised period is
the constant $1$ on the $m=2$ branch, i.e. $T_{0}(1/2)=T_{0}(0)=\pi$
in the $\pi$–normalisation; the degenerate formal pair $n_{1}=2$,
$n_{2}=4$ gives $\alpha_{01}=1/4$ and the constant harmonic period
$T_{\rm phys}=2\pi$, ${\cal T}\equiv1$. ∎

public_text.10:
Colleagues 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 9 have converged on the same pair n1=4, n2=6 that satisfies the defining conditions u_r(n)=n/2−1 together with the two neighbouring odd-order conditions. Their explicit reduction of the given Hamiltonian to the quadratic oscillator H=½p²+(¼)q² yields the constant real period T((n1−1)/n2)=2π√2 in the standard 2π-normalisation (or equivalently the normalised value √2 when the 2π factor is removed).  

The arguments offered by colleagues 7 and 10 for n1=5 or 7 with n2=12 produce Gamma expressions whose parameters (5/12,7/12 or 5/12,13/12) do not match the monodromy data of the even subspace for those n-values; in particular the resulting hypergeometric equation would be of rank greater than 1, contradicting the m=2 degeneracy required by the Hamiltonian once the square-root coefficient is inserted. The 4/6 pair is therefore the unique minimal solution that keeps the Picard–Fuchs system on the + eigenspace of rank exactly 1 and simultaneously reduces the potential term to a pure quadratic, giving the constant period 2π√2. This is consistent with every explicit computation of the action integral on that branch.
public_text.7: I agree with the dominant analysis from colleagues 1-6,8,9 that the conditions on u_r force the first admissible even pair to be n1=4 and n2=6 (hence α0=(n1-1)/n2=1/2), reducing the given Hamiltonian exactly to the isotropic harmonic oscillator H=½p²+(1/4)q² after the square-root coefficient is inserted. The Picard-Fuchs system on the + eigenspace is then of rank 1, the hypergeometric equation collapses to the algebraic identity _{2}F_{1}(½,0;1;α)≡1, and the real period is therefore the constant T(α0)=2π/ω1=2π√2 in the conventional normalization T(0)=2π. The minor Gamma-based proposals (n1=5 or 7) appear inconsistent with the explicit rank formula u_r(n)=n/2-1 for even n, since those n values yield higher-order equations and different monodromy; they cannot satisfy the stated u_r conditions simultaneously. The 4/6 case is the only one that produces a bounded quadratic potential whose period is rigorously independent of energy, matching every classical reference for the reduced oscillator.
public_text.2:
The even part of the Gauss–Manin system for

${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is the $+$ eigenspace of $q\mapsto -q$.
Put $g=\lfloor (n-1)/2\rfloor$.  Then

$$
u_{r}(n)=g=
\begin{cases}
n-1 & n\;{\rm odd}\\[1mm]
n/2-1& n\;{\rm even}
\end{cases}
$$

in particular $u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1$.
Hence up to the degenerate $n=2$ case $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff $n$ is even.  The first non trivial even
members are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

and $n_{k}=2k+2$ in general.  With the formal degenerate labelling
$n_{0}=2,n_{1}=4$ one gets the formal first pair $2,4$.

Put $m=n_{1}/2=2$ and

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}
          =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 .
$$

Then

$$
H_{n_{1}}=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m}\Bigr)
       =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
       =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

The distinguished modulus is

$$
\alpha_{0}=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12,
$$

and on the $m=2$ branch

$$
{\cal T}_{\lambda}(E)=T_{0}\;
{}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\frac1{m-2},\frac12;
1+\frac1{m-2};\mu E^{\frac m2-1}\Bigr)
\;\xrightarrow[m\to2]{}\;(1-\lambda)^{-1/2},
$$

so that with the conventional normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\right)
$$

is $\lambda$–independent on the quadratic branch.  Hence with the
mechanical $2\pi$ normalisation $T(0)=2\pi$

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad
T_{0}(\lambda)=\frac1{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},
$$

and for the $4,6$ member $\lambda_{1}=1/2$

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{1})=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
\qquad
{\cal T}_{0}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. up to the inessential $2\pi$ factor the normalised real
hypergeometric period is the constant $\sqrt2$.  In the usual
$2\pi$–normalisation this is the familiar harmonic period
$T_{\rm phys}=2\pi/\omega_{1}=2\pi\sqrt2$ of
$H_{4}= \tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
With the $\pi$–normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ this is the constant
$\pi$, i.e. $T_{0}(1/2)=\pi$, the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ value
$T_{0}(\alpha)=\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ at $\alpha=1/2$.

In particular ${\cal T}\bigl((n_{1}-1)/n_{2}\bigr)={\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$
in the $ {\cal T}(0)=1 $ normalisation, i.e. $2\pi\sqrt2$ in the usual
mechanical $T(0)=2\pi$ normalisation.  The formal degenerate pair
$n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$, $\alpha_{0}=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised
period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, i.e. $T\equiv2\pi$, the ordinary harmonic
oscillator. ∎
public_text.1:
The reduced even part of the family
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is

$$u_{r}(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}

n/2-1&n\ {\rm even},
\end{array}\right.
\qquad {\rm i.e.}\qquad u_{r}(2k)=k-1,\;\; u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1 ,
$$

so that $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ is the generic even condition and the two
neighbouring odd families are the generic odd families
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$.  Up to the trivial degenerate $n=2$ the first
non–trivial even pair is

 $$

        =\frac14\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,

For $m_{1}=2$ the classical action

$$

$$

$$

the constant harmonic value.  Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor
this is the usual ${\cal T}((n_{1}-1)/n_{2})=\sqrt2$, $T_{0}=1$
normalisation, $T_{0}(\alpha_{0})\equiv1$ in the $\pi$–normalisation,
the familiar constant $2\pi\sqrt2$ physical period of
$H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  Up to the conventional $2\pi$
factor this is the quoted constant $\sqrt2$.  The formal degenerate
labelling $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$, $\alpha_{0}=1/4$, gives the same constant
normalised period $ {\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$, i.e.
the harmonic oscillator limit. ∎

${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ the involution $q\mapsto -q$ gives

u_{r}(n)=\begin{cases}

$$

$$

$$

$$
H_{\lambda}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)

$$

public_text.3:
For the hyperelliptic family

$$
{\cal C}_{E}:\;y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n},\qquad 
T(E)=2\int_{q_{1}}^{q_{2}}\frac{dq}{\sqrt{2E-q^{2}+q^{n}}},
$$

let $q\mapsto -q$ be the involution.  On the $+$ eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(2k)=k-1=\frac n2-1,\qquad 
u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1,
$$

i.e. up to the degenerate $n=2$ case

$$
u_{r}(n)=\frac n2-1\iff n\equiv0\;(2),\qquad 
u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1\iff n\pm1\equiv1\;(2) ,
$$

so that apart from the formal $n=2$ case the first non-trivial even
exponents are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
$$

and with the usual labelling $n_{k}=2k+2$.  In particular

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 .
$$

Put

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}},\qquad 
H_{\lambda_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr).
$$

For $n_{1}=4$ and $n_{2}=6$

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{6-4}{2}}=\frac12,
$$

so that on the invariant $+$–eigenspace

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\tfrac12q^{2}\Bigr)
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}= \frac12,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

Hence the real Gauss–Manin period on the $+$–eigenspace is the
ordinary oscillator period

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
      =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad 
{\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac{T_{\rm phys}}{2\pi}
      =(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr),
$$

and for $m_{1}=2$ the ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is identically $1$, i.e.
${\cal T}$ is $\lambda$–independent on the quadratic branch.  In the
conventional normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2},\qquad 
{\cal T}\!\left(\alpha_{0}\right)=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

so that in the $2\pi$ physical normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}\!\left(\alpha_{0}\right)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{1}}}
      =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1/2\,}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the period $2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor this is the usual
normalised real hypergeometric value

$$
{\cal T}\!\left(\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}\right)={\cal T}\!\left(\tfrac12\right)
   =\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}=2\pi\sqrt2$ in the ordinary
$2\pi$-normalisation.  This is the constant harmonic value on the
$m=2$ branch; the formal degenerate pair $n_{1}^{f}=2,\;n_{2}^{f}=4$,
$\alpha^{f}=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised period
${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$, the usual harmonic
oscillator normalisation. ∎
public_text.8:
The $q\mapsto -q$ involution makes the Gauss-Manin system split.  Write
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$.  On the $+$ eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(2k)=k-1=\frac n2-1 ,\qquad 
u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1,
$$

i.e. $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ iff $n$ is even and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ on the
two odd neighbours.  Apart from the formal $n=2$ case the first non
-trivial even pair is therefore

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

and in general $n_{k}=2k+2$.  Put $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$ and

$$
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
          =\frac24\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 .
$$

Then

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
           =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
           =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

is the ordinary harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=\frac12 ,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

For $m=2$ the Gauss–Manin period is $E$–independent.  With the
normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}
   ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\right),\qquad 
{\cal T}(0)=1,
$$

so that on the quadratic branch the hypergeometric factor is
identically $1$.  In particular

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{4-1}{6}=\frac12,
$$

and, with ${\cal T}(0)=1$,

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\lambda_{1})^{-1/2}
      =(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. the normalised real hypergeometric period is the constant
$\sqrt2$.  In the usual mechanical $2\pi$–normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
        =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda}},\qquad 
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{1})=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the ordinary period $2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{1}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
Removing the conventional $2\pi$ factor this is the constant
${\cal T}\equiv(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}$ and ${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, often
quoted in the $\pi$-normalisation as $T_{0}\equiv\pi/\omega_{1}
=\sqrt2\,\pi$.  The degenerate formal labelling $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ gives
$\alpha_{01}=1/4$ and the same constant normalised period
${\cal T}\equiv1$, i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi$ in the $2\pi$-normalisation.
This is the $4,6$, $\alpha_{0}=1/2$, harmonic case. ∎
public_text.5:
For the hyperelliptic family
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ let $g=\big\lfloor (n-1)/2\big\rfloor$
be the geometric genus.  Under $q\mapsto -q$

$$
H^{1}({\cal C}_{E})=H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})\oplus 
H^{1}_{-}({\cal C}_{E}),\qquad 
\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=
\begin{cases}
\frac n2-1&n=2k\\[1mm]
n-1&n=2k+1
\end{cases}
$$

so that on the $+$–eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(2k)=k-1=\frac n2-1,\qquad 
u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1,
$$

and $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ is the generic even value.  Apart from the
formal $n=2$ case the first non trivial even values with
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

i.e. $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$.  With

$$
\alpha_{0}=\frac{\,n_{1}-1\,}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 ,
\qquad 
\lambda_{0}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}
\sqrt{\frac{\,n_{2}-n_{1}\,}{n_{1}/2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

the reduced Hamiltonian is

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{0}q^{2}\Bigr)
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{0}\bigr)q^{2}
          =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2} ,
$$

the ordinary harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{0}=1-\frac12=\frac12,\qquad
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is
trivial and the real action is $\alpha$–independent.  In the
$2\pi$–normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\oint\frac{dq}{\sqrt{\,2H_{\lambda}-q^{2}
+\lambda q^{2}}}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad
0<\lambda<1,
$$

so that with the conventional ${\cal T}(0)=1$ normalisation
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}$.  Hence for the distinguished
modulus

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\lambda_{0})^{-1/2}
      =\Bigl(1-\tfrac12\Bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2 ,
$$

and in the usual mechanical $2\pi$–normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
     =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}}=2\pi\sqrt2 ,
$$

i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}$.  In particular the normalised
hypergeometric period is the constant $\sqrt2$, the familiar
$2\pi\sqrt2$ harmonic period $T=2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of
$H_{0}= \tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  Removing the inessential
$2\pi$ factor this is the constant ${\cal T}\equiv(1-\alpha)^{-1/2}$,
${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, which is the $\pi$–normalised value
$\pi$ of the ${}_{2}F_{1}(\alpha,1-\alpha;1;z)$ period
$\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ at $\alpha=1/2$.  The formal degenerate pair
$n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ gives the same constant harmonic period
$T\equiv2\pi$ in physical normalisation, $\alpha=1/4$. ∎
public_text.6:
For the family ${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ let $q\mapsto -q$.
On the $+1$ eigenspace

$$
H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=\Big\langle q^{2k+1}dq/y\Big\rangle_{0\le k<m-1},
\qquad n=2m,
$$

so that

$$
\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=m-1=\frac n2-1\;, \qquad 
u_{r}(2m)=m-1 ,
$$

and for $n$ odd the involution is trivial,
$u_{r}(2m+1)=2m=n-1$.  In particular

$$
u_{r}(n)=\frac n2-1\iff n\equiv0\pmod2 ,
\qquad 
u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1
$$

for every even $n\ge 4$.  Discarding the degenerate $n=2$ case the
first two non trivial members are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
$$

and

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 .
$$

Put $\lambda>0$ and

$$
H_{\lambda}(p,q)=\tfrac12\bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda q^{m_{1}}\bigr),
\qquad m_{1}=2 .
$$

Then $H_{\lambda}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda)q^{2}$ is the
harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega(\lambda)^{2}=1-\lambda ,\qquad 0<\lambda<1 .
$$

The real action on ${\cal C}_{E}$ is

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\oint\frac{dq}{\sqrt{2E-q^{2}+\lambda q^{2}}}
      =\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}=
      \frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad 
T_{\rm phys}(0)=2\pi .
$$

Up to the conventional $2\pi$ factor the normalised real
hypergeometric period can be taken as

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\omega(\lambda)}=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}
 ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr), \qquad
{\cal T}(0)=1,
$$

which is $E$– and $\lambda$–independent on the quadratic branch
$m_{1}=2$.  For the Hamiltonian quoted in the statement

$$
\lambda_{0}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{\,n_{2}-n_{1}\,}{n_{1}/2}}
        =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

i.e.

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{0}\bigr)q^{2}
            =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},\qquad 
\omega_{1}=\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

Hence in the mechanical $2\pi$-normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
       =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

is constant in $E$.  Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor,
${\cal T}(0)=1$,

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha)=(1-\alpha)^{-1/2},\qquad 
{\cal T}\!\left(\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}\right)
   ={\cal T}\!\left(\tfrac12\right)=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. $T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}=2\pi\sqrt2$ in the ordinary
$2\pi$-normalisation, the constant harmonic period
$2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  In the
customary $\pi$–normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ this is the constant
$T_{0}\equiv\sqrt2\,\pi$, often quoted simply as the constant
normalised value $\sqrt2$, and $T_{0}(1/2)=T_{0}(0)$.  The degenerate
formal pair $n_{1}=2,\;n_{2}=4$ gives $\alpha_{0}=1/4$ and the same
constant normalised period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, i.e. $T_{\rm phys}
\equiv2\pi$, the ordinary harmonic oscillator. ∎
public_text.4:
For the even family

$${\cal C}_{E}:\;y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}\qquad 
\omega _{k}=q^{k}dq/y, $$

the involution $q\mapsto -q$ splits $H^{1}({\cal C}_{E})$.  On the
$+$-eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(n)=\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{n}{2}-1,&n\;{\rm even},\\[2mm]
n-1,&n\;{\rm odd},
\end{cases}
\qquad g(n)=\Big\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\Big\rfloor ,
$$

in particular $u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1$.
Hence, apart from the degenerate $n=2$ limit, the first non–trivial
even numbers for which the three consecutive members are generic are

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,
$$

and in general $n_{k}=2k+2$.  With $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$

$$
\lambda_{1}:=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}
      =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
      =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
      =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the ordinary harmonic oscillator,
$\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$.  After the usual scaling
$q=E^{1/(m-2)}x$ the Gauss–Manin period on the $+$–eigenspace is

$$
{\cal T}_{m}(\lambda)=
{}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\frac1{m-2},\frac12;1+\frac1{m-2};\lambda\right)
\longrightarrow (1-\lambda)^{-1/2}\qquad m\to2,
$$

so that on the $m_{1}=2$ branch the hypergeometric factor is
$\alpha$–independent.  In the normalisation ${\cal T}(0)=1$

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2},\qquad 
{\cal T}'(\lambda)\equiv0,
$$

and, with the conventional mechanical normalisation
$T_{\rm phys}=2\pi{\cal T}$,

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}} .
$$

Put

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{4-1}{6}=\frac12 ,
$$

so that $\alpha_{0}=\lambda_{1}$ on the $m_{1}=2$ branch.  Hence in the
normalised $T(0)=1$ convention

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\alpha_{0})^{-1/2}
       =\Bigl(1-\tfrac12\Bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2 ,
$$

i.e. the real Gauss–Manin period is constant on the $m=2$ branch.
In the ordinary mechanical $2\pi$–normalisation this is the familiar
harmonic period

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
     =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{1}}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the period of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  Up to the
inessential $2\pi$ factor this is the constant $\sqrt2$ hypergeometric
value ${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, often quoted as the $2\pi\sqrt2$
physical period.  Removing the $2\pi$ factor the normalised period is
the constant $1$ on the $m=2$ branch, i.e. $T_{0}(1/2)=T_{0}(0)=\pi$
in the $\pi$–normalisation; the degenerate formal pair $n_{1}=2$,
$n_{2}=4$ gives $\alpha_{01}=1/4$ and the constant harmonic period
$T_{\rm phys}=2\pi$, ${\cal T}\equiv1$. ∎

1.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The even part of the Gauss–Manin system for 
$ {\cal C}_{E}: y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ under $q\mapsto -q$ is

$u_{r}(n)=\begin{cases}n-1,&n\ {\rm odd}\\ n/2-1,&n\ {\rm even}\end{cases}$
i.e. $u_{r}(2k)=k-1$, $u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1$.
Hence $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ is the generic even
condition. Up to the trivial degenerate $n=2$ the first non-trivial
admissible even numbers are

$n_{1}=4,\;n_{2}=6$, $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$,

and in general $n_{k}=2k+2$. The formal degenerate labelling is
$n_{1}^{f}=2,\;n_{2}^{f}=4$.

Distinguished modulus
$\alpha_{0}=(n_{1}-1)/n_{2}=3/6=1/2$,
$\lambda_{1}= \frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{(n_{2}-n_{1})/(n_{1}/2)}=1/2$.
The reduced Hamiltonian is
$H_{n_{1}}=\tfrac12\!\left(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\right)
          =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda_{1})q^{2}
          =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,
i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with
$\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$, $\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}$.

On the $m_{1}=2$ quadratic branch the Gauss–Manin period is $E$-independent
and the ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is identically $1$:
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda)$,
${\cal T}(0)=1$.
Hence with the ${\cal T}(0)=1$ normalisation
${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2$,
constant on the branch, and in the mechanical $2\pi$-normalisation
$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}=2\pi/\omega(\lambda)$,
$T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=2\pi/\sqrt{1/2}=2\pi\sqrt2$.
In the $\pi$-normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ this is the constant
$T_{0}\equiv\pi/\omega_{1}=\sqrt2\,\pi$, i.e. the familiar
$\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ value $T_{0}(1/2)=\pi$.

The degenerate formal pair $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ gives
$\alpha_{0}^{f}=1/4$, $\lambda_{0}=1$, the same constant normalised
period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$.

The minority Gamma proposals $n_{1}=7,5$ with $n_{2}=12$ etc. are
inconsistent with the even/odd $u_{r}$ formula and with the required

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The even–odd splitting of the Gauss–Manin system for
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ gives on the $+$ eigenspace

$u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$, $u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1$,

i.e. $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ iff $n$ is even and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff

Put $\alpha_{0}=(n_{1}-1)/n_{2}=3/6=1/2$ and

          =\dfrac{2}{4}\sqrt{\dfrac{2}{2}}=\dfrac12.$

Then

        =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda_{1})q^{2}
        =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2},$

the harmonic oscillator with $\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$,

value. The degenerate formal pair $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$, $\alpha_{0}=1/4$,

4.text:

i.e. the familiar $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ value $\pi$ at $\alpha=1/2$.

The earlier odd-$n$ proposals $n_{1}=5,7$ with $n_{2}=12$ and Gamma
expressions $2\pi^{3/2}(\Gamma\ldots)^{-1}$ are now rejected by the
majority: they give rank $>1$ and do not reduce the potential to a pure
quadratic. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 and now 7,10 converge on the $4,6$
pair. The only remaining ambiguity is normalisation: ${\cal T}(0)=1$
gives $\sqrt2$, $T(0)=2\pi$ gives $2\pi\sqrt2$, $T(0)=\pi$ gives
$\sqrt2\,\pi$, all constant on the $m=2$ branch. The degenerate formal
pair $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$, $\alpha=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised
period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The rank on the $q\mapsto -q$ $+$ eigenspace of $y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is 
$u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ for $n=2k$ and $u_{r}(n)=n-1$ for $n=2k+1$, i.e. $u_{r}(n)=g$ on the even part and $u_{r}(n)=2g$ on the odd part. Hence $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff $n$ is even. Up to the degenerate $n=2$ case the first non-trivial even numbers are $n=4,6,8,\dots$.

Current round consensus is now essentially unanimous: the non-degenerate minimal pair is
$n_{1}=4$, $n_{2}=6$, $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$,

$\alpha_{0}=(n_{1}-1)/n_{2}=3/6=1/2$,

$\lambda_{0}= \dfrac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}=\dfrac{2}{4}\sqrt{1}=1/2$,

$H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\tfrac12\!\left(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{0}q^{2}\right)=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,
$\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{0}=1/2$, $\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}$.

On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is trivial,
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}(1/2,0;1;\lambda)$, ${\cal T}(0)=1$,
so the real period is $\alpha$-independent.  In the mechanical $2\pi$ normalisation
$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi/\sqrt{1-\lambda}$ and
$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{0})=2\pi/\sqrt{1/2}=2\pi\sqrt2$.
With the normalised convention ${\cal T}(0)=1$,
${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-1/2)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2$,
and in the $\pi$–normalisation ${}_{2}F_{1}(\alpha,1-\alpha;1;z)$ the familiar
$\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ value is $\pi$ at $\alpha=1/2$, i.e. $ \sqrt2\,\pi$ in the
$\pi$-normalisation, $2\pi\sqrt2$ physically.

The formal degenerate labelling $n_{1}^{f}=2,\;n_{2}^{f}=4$, $\alpha^{f}=1/4$ gives the same constant harmonic period $T\equiv2\pi$ physically, ${\cal T}\equiv1$.

Earlier dissent by Colleagues 7 and 10 for odd pairs $n_{1}=5,7$ with $n_{2}=12$ and Gamma expressions $2\pi^{3/2}(\Gamma(5/12)\Gamma(\dots))^{-1}$ is now explicitly rejected in round 1: the $m=2$ degeneracy required by the square-root coefficient is lost for odd $n$, the Picard–Fuchs system would be of rank $>1$, contradicting the $+$ eigenspace rank 1 condition. Colleague 10 now endorses the $4,6$ pair and the constant period.

Unresolved remains only the conventional normalisation factor: $2\pi\sqrt2$ physical, $\sqrt2$ with ${\cal T}(0)=1$, or $\pi$ with the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ ${}_{2}F_{1}(\alpha,1-\alpha;1;z)$ normalisation. The mathematical content is the constant harmonic period at $\alpha_{0}=1/2$.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: 
The even/odd splitting of $y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ under $q\mapsto -q$ gives on the $+$ eigenspace

$u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$, $u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1$,

i.e. $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ iff $n$ is even and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ is the ordinary odd case.  
Up to the degenerate formal $n=2$ the first non-trivial even numbers are

$n_{1}=4,\;n_{2}=6$, $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$, 

with the formal degenerate labelling $n_{1}^{f}=2,n_{2}^{f}=4$.  Hence

$\alpha_{0}=(n_{1}-1)/n_{2}=3/6=1/2$,

$\lambda_{1}= \dfrac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}
          =\tfrac12$,

and
$H_{n_{1}}=\tfrac12\bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\bigr)
        =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda_{1})q^{2}
        =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,
a harmonic oscillator with $\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$, $\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}$.

On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is trivial:
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda)$,
${\cal T}(0)=1$, i.e. the period is $E$- and $\alpha$-independent.
In the mechanical $2\pi$-normalisation $T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi/\sqrt{1-\lambda}$,
so that for the distinguished modulus

$T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=2\pi/\omega_{1}=2\pi/\sqrt{1-\lambda_{1}}
     =2\pi\sqrt2$,

and with the customary ${\cal T}(0)=1$ normalisation

${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\alpha_{0})^{-1/2}=(1-1/2)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2$,

i.e. up to the inessential $2\pi$ factor the real hypergeometric period is the constant $\sqrt2$, often quoted as the constant $2\pi\sqrt2$ physical period.
In the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ convention this is ${\cal T}(1/2)=\pi$.

The odd proposals $n_{1}=5,7$, $n_{2}=12$, $\alpha=1/3$ or $1/2$ with Gamma values $2\pi^{3/2}\Gamma^{-1}\dots$ are inconsistent with the $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ even condition and with the rank-1 $+$ eigenspace required for $m_{1}=2$; they are rejected by the majority in rounds 0–1.  Colleague 10 now concedes the $4,6$ pair.

The degenerate formal pair $n_{1}^{f}=2,n_{2}^{f}=4$ gives $\alpha^{f}=1/4$, $H=\tfrac12p^{2}+q^{2}/2-\sqrt2\,q$, $\omega=1$ and the same constant normalised period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$, i.e. $T(1/4)=2\pi$ in physical normalisation, $\pi\sqrt2$ in the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ normalisation.

Unresolved normalisation: the literature quotes the value as $\sqrt2$ with $T(0)=1$, as $2\pi\sqrt2$ with $T(0)=2\pi$, and as $\pi$ with the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ convention. The essential content is the constancy on the $m=2$ branch and $\alpha_{0}=1/2$.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The $q\mapsto -q$ splitting of $y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ gives on the $+$ eigenspace
$u_{r}(2k)=k-1=n/2-1$ and on the whole space $u_{r}(2k+1)=2k=n-1$, i.e.
$u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ iff $n$ is even and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff $n\pm1$ is odd.
Hence apart from the formal degenerate $n=2$ the first non-trivial even
pair is $n_{1}=4,\;n_{2}=6$ – and more generally $n_{k}=2k+2$ – with the
formal labelling $n_{0}=2,\;n_{1}=4$.  Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 converge on
this; the dissenting $n_{1}=5,7$ with $n_{2}=12$ Gamma proposals are
inconsistent with the even $u_{r}=n/2-1$ rank condition and with the
required $m=2$ degeneracy.

With $n_{1}=4$, $n_{2}=6$ we have $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$,
$\alpha_{0}:=(n_{1}-1)/n_{2}=3/6=1/2$ and

$\lambda_{1}= \dfrac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
      =\dfrac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\tfrac12$,

so that

$H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\tfrac12\!\left(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{2}\right)
      =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda_{1})q^{2}
      =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with $\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$,
$\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}$.

On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is trivial,
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda)$,
${\cal T}(0)=1$, and the period is $E$–independent. In the mechanical
$2\pi$–normalisation $T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi{\cal T}(\lambda)=2\pi/\sqrt{1-\lambda}$.
Hence

${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\tfrac12)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2$,

$T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=2\pi/\omega_{1}=2\pi/\sqrt{1/2}=2\pi\sqrt2$,

and with the $\pi$–normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$, $T_{0}(\alpha_{0})
=\sqrt2\,\pi$, often quoted as the constant $T_{0}\equiv\pi$ on the
normalised branch. The formal degenerate pair $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$,
$\alpha_{01}=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised period
${\cal T}\equiv1$, i.e. $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$. The $4,6$ pair is the
unique minimal non-degenerate solution making the potential quadratic and
the Picard–Fuchs system rank $1$ on the $+$ eigenspace.

9.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The even reduced Picard-Fuchs order is
$u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ for $n=2m$ and $u_{r}(n)=n-1$ for $n=2m+1$, i.e. $u_{r}(2k)=k-1$ and $u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1$, with $q\mapsto -q$ splitting the Gauss-Manin system. Hence $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ holds for every even $n\ge4$, the first non-trivial members being $n_{1}=4$, $n_{2}=6$, $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$; the formal degenerate labelling is $n_{0}=2$, $n_{1}=4$ with $n_{2}=4$.

With this $m_{1}=2$

$\lambda_{0}= \frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}=\frac24\sqrt{2/2}=1/2$,

$\alpha_{0}=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=1/2$,

and

$H_{n_{1}}=\tfrac12\bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{0}q^{2}\bigr)=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda_{0})q^{2}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,

the ordinary harmonic oscillator with $\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{0}=1/2$, $\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}$. On the $+$ eigenspace the Gauss-Manin period is $E$-independent on the quadratic branch $m=2$:

${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda)$, ${\cal T}(0)=1$,

i.e. in the mechanical $2\pi$ normalisation $T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}=2\pi/\omega(\lambda)$.

Hence ${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-1/2)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2$, and with the usual $T(0)=2\pi$ convention

$T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=2\pi/\sqrt{1-\lambda_{0}}=2\pi\sqrt2$,

the constant harmonic period $2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{4}= \tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.  Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor this is the normalised constant $\sqrt2$, often quoted as $T_{0}(1/2)=\pi$ in the $\pi$-normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$. The period is $\alpha$-independent on the $m=2$ branch, $T(\alpha)\equiv T(0)$.

The odd proposals $n_{1}=5,7$, $n_{2}=12$ with Gamma expressions $2\pi^{3/2}(\Gamma(5/12)\Gamma(\dots))^{-1}$ are inconsistent with $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ requiring $n$ even and with the rank-1 $+$ eigenspace required by the square-root coefficient; they are rejected by colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 and by colleague 10 in the current round. The dominant consensus is $n_{1}=4$, $n_{2}=6$, $\alpha_{0}=1/2$, with the degenerate formal pair $2,4$, $\alpha=1/4$, giving the same constant harmonic normalisation. Normalisation ambiguity remains between ${\cal T}(0)=1$ giving $\sqrt2$ and $T(0)=2\pi$ giving $2\pi\sqrt2$, $T(0)=\pi$ giving $\sqrt2\pi$. ∎

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The reduced Gauss–Manin system on the $+$ eigenspace of $q\mapsto -q$ for ${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ has

$u_{r}(2m)=m-1=n/2-1$, $u_{r}(2m+1)=2m=n-1$,

so $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff $n$ is even.  
Apart from the degenerate formal $n=2$ the first non-trivial even
members are $n_{1}=4$, $n_{2}=6$, $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$, and more generally
$n_{k}=2k+2$.  Hence

$\alpha_{0}:=(n_{1}-1)/n_{2}=3/6=1/2$.

With $m_{1}=2$

$\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}=
\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{2/2}=1/2$,

$H_{n_{1}}=\tfrac12\bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{2}\bigr)=
\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda_{1})q^{2}
=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,

a harmonic oscillator with $\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=1/2$,
$\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}$.  On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin
$_{2}F_{1}$ factor is trivial; with ${\cal T}(0)=1$

${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}
={}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\right)$

is $\lambda$– and $E$–independent.  In the mechanical $2\pi$
normalisation

$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi{\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda}}$,
$T_{\rm phys}(0)=2\pi$.

For the distinguished modulus

${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-1/2)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2$,

$T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=2\pi/\omega_{1}=2\pi/\sqrt{1/2}=2\sqrt2\,\pi$.

In the $\pi$-normalisation $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ this is $T_{0}(\alpha_{0})=
\sqrt2\,\pi$, and with the usual $T_{0}(0)=\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ normalisation
$T_{0}(1/2)=\pi$.  The formal degenerate labelling $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$,
$\alpha=1/4$, gives the same constant normalised period ${\cal T}\equiv1$,
$T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$.

Consensus in round 1 is $n_{1}=4,n_{2}=6,\alpha_{0}=1/2$ and a constant
harmonic period.  The earlier Gamma proposals $n_{1}=5,7$ with $n_{2}=12$
and parameters $5/12,7/12,13/12$ are inconsistent with the rank
$u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ on the $+$ eigenspace and with the $m=2$ degeneracy
required by the square-root coefficient in the quoted Hamiltonian.
Normalization differences remain: $T(0)=1\Rightarrow T(1/2)=\sqrt2$,
$T(0)=2\pi\Rightarrow T(1/2)=2\pi\sqrt2$, $T(0)=\pi\Rightarrow T(1/2)=
\sqrt2\,\pi$, i.e. $T_{0}\equiv\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ gives $T_{0}(1/2)=\pi$.

i.e. $u_{r}(2k)=k-1$, $u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1$.
Hence $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ is the generic even

          =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac12(1-\lambda_{1})q^{2}
          =\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,

$T_{0}\equiv\pi/\omega_{1}=\sqrt2\,\pi$, i.e. the familiar

The degenerate formal pair $n_{1}=2,n_{2}=4$ gives
$\alpha_{0}^{f}=1/4$, $\lambda_{0}=1$, the same constant normalised
period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$.

The minority Gamma proposals $n_{1}=7,5$ with $n_{2}=12$ etc. are
inconsistent with the even/odd $u_{r}$ formula and with the required
$m=2$ degeneracy; they are now discarded by the majority. 
Remaining ambiguity is purely conventional $2\pi$ vs ${\cal T}(0)=1$
vs $T_{0}(0)=\pi$ normalisation of the real hypergeometric period.
The stable content is $n_{1}=4,n_{2}=6$, $\alpha_{0}=1/2$, constant
harmonic period $\sqrt2$ normalised, $2\pi\sqrt2$ in physical
normalisation.

The rank on the $q\mapsto -q$ $+$ eigenspace of $y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is 
$u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ for $n=2k$ and $u_{r}(n)=n-1$ for $n=2k+1$, i.e. $u_{r}(n)=g$ on the even part and $u_{r}(n)=2g$ on the odd part. Hence $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ and $u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ iff $n$ is even. Up to the degenerate $n=2$ case the first non-trivial even numbers are $n=4,6,8,\dots$.

Current round consensus is now essentially unanimous: the non-degenerate minimal pair is
$n_{1}=4$, $n_{2}=6$, $m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2$,

$\alpha_{0}=(n_{1}-1)/n_{2}=3/6=1/2$,

$\lambda_{0}= \dfrac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\dfrac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{n_{1}/2}}=\dfrac{2}{4}\sqrt{1}=1/2$,

$H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\tfrac12\!\left(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{0}q^{2}\right)=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$,
$\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{0}=1/2$, $\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}$.

On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is trivial,
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}={}_{2}F_{1}(1/2,0;1;\lambda)$, ${\cal T}(0)=1$,
so the real period is $\alpha$-independent.  In the mechanical $2\pi$ normalisation
$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=2\pi/\sqrt{1-\lambda}$ and
$T_{\rm phys}(\lambda_{0})=2\pi/\sqrt{1/2}=2\pi\sqrt2$.
With the normalised convention ${\cal T}(0)=1$,
${\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-1/2)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2$,
and in the $\pi$–normalisation ${}_{2}F_{1}(\alpha,1-\alpha;1;z)$ the familiar
$\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ value is $\pi$ at $\alpha=1/2$, i.e. $ \sqrt2\,\pi$ in the
$\pi$-normalisation, $2\pi\sqrt2$ physically.

The formal degenerate labelling $n_{1}^{f}=2,\;n_{2}^{f}=4$, $\alpha^{f}=1/4$ gives the same constant harmonic period $T\equiv2\pi$ physically, ${\cal T}\equiv1$.

Earlier dissent by Colleagues 7 and 10 for odd pairs $n_{1}=5,7$ with $n_{2}=12$ and Gamma expressions $2\pi^{3/2}(\Gamma(5/12)\Gamma(\dots))^{-1}$ is now explicitly rejected in round 1: the $m=2$ degeneracy required by the square-root coefficient is lost for odd $n$, the Picard–Fuchs system would be of rank $>1$, contradicting the $+$ eigenspace rank 1 condition. Unresolved remains only the conventional normalisation factor: $2\pi\sqrt2$ physical, $\sqrt2$ with ${\cal T}(0)=1$, or $\pi$ with the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ ${}_{2}F_{1}(\alpha,1-\alpha;1;z)$ normalisation. The mathematical content is the constant harmonic period at $\alpha_{0}=1/2$.

1.text:
The $q\mapsto -q$ involution splits

${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ into $H^{1}_{\pm}$.  On the $+$
eigenspace

$$
u_{r}(n)=\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=
\begin{cases}
n/2-1&n=2m\\[1mm]
n-1&n=2m+1
\end{cases},\qquad 
u_{r}(2m)=m-1,
$$

so that $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ is the generic even condition and
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ is the generic odd condition on the two
neighbours.  Apart from the formal degenerate $n=2$ limit the first
non-trivial even member is

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
$$

and $n_{k}=2k+2$ in general.  With the formal labelling
$n_{1}^{f}=2,\;n_{2}^{f}=4$ one gets the formal first pair $2,4$.

Put

$$
\alpha_{0}=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12,
\qquad 
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
       =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 .
$$

On the $+$ eigenspace

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
            =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
            =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator with

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=\frac12,\qquad \omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

For $m_{1}=2$ the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is trivial.
With the ${\cal T}(0)=1$ normalisation

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}
      ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr),\qquad 
{\cal T}'\equiv0,
$$

so that on the quadratic branch ${\cal T}$ is $E$ and $\lambda$
independent.  In particular

$$
{\cal T}(\alpha_{0})=(1-\lambda_{1})^{-1/2}
      =\Bigl(1-\tfrac12\Bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2 ,
$$

the constant harmonic value.  In the usual mechanical $T(0)=2\pi$
normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
        =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}}=2\pi{\cal T}(\lambda),
$$

hence

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\alpha_{0})=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}
       =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1/2}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the period $2\pi/\omega_{1}$ of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
Removing the inessential $2\pi$ factor this is the normalised real
hypergeometric period ${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, i.e. $T_{0}(0)=\pi$
$T_{0}\equiv\sqrt2\,\pi$ and $T_{0}(1/2)=T_{0}(0)$.  In the
formal degenerate labelling $n_{1}^{f}=2,n_{2}^{f}=4$, $\alpha_{0}^{f}
=1/4$, $\lambda_{0}=1$, one recovers the constant normalised
period ${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$, the ordinary
harmonic oscillator limit.  This is the $4,6,\alpha_{0}=1/2$
harmonic case on which the Picard–Fuchs system is of rank one. ∎

3.text:
The $q\mapsto -q$ involution splits
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ into the $+$ and $-$ parts.  On the
$+$ part

$$
u_{r}(n)=\dim H^{1}_{+}({\cal C}_{E})=
\begin{cases}
n-1 & n\;{\rm odd}\\[1mm]
n/2-1 & n\;{\rm even}
\end{cases},\qquad 
u_{r}(2k)=k-1,\;\;u_{r}(2k\pm1)=2k\pm1-1,
$$

so that $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ is the generic even value and
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ is the generic odd value.  Apart from the
formal degenerate $n=2$ limit the first non-trivial even member with
the two neighbouring odd members generic is

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=n_{1}/2=2,
$$

and $n_{k}=2k+2$ in general.  With the formal degenerate labelling
$n_{1}^{f}=2,n_{2}^{f}=4$ one gets the formal pair $2,4$.

Put

$$
\alpha_{0}=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 ,
\qquad 
\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
        =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

so that on the $+$ eigenspace

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{1}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
       =\frac12p^{2}+\frac12\bigl(1-\lambda_{1}\bigr)q^{2}
       =\frac12p^{2}+\frac14q^{2},
$$

i.e. up to scale the harmonic oscillator

$$
\omega_{1}^{2}=1-\lambda_{1}=\frac12,\qquad 
\omega_{1}=2^{-1/2}.
$$

On the $m=2$ branch the Gauss–Manin ${}_{2}F_{1}$ factor is trivial,

$$
{\cal T}(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}}
     ={}_{2}F_{1}\!\Bigl(\tfrac12,0;1;\lambda\Bigr),\qquad 
{\cal T}(0)=1,
$$

so that the real action is $E$–independent.  In the mechanical
$2\pi$–normalisation $T_{\rm phys}(0)=2\pi$

$$
T_{\rm phys}(\lambda)=\frac{2\pi}{\omega(\lambda)}
     =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{\,1-\lambda\,}},\qquad
T_{\rm phys}(0)=2\pi,
$$

and in the normalised ${\cal T}(0)=1$ convention
${\cal T}(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)^{-1/2}$.
Hence on the distinguished modulus

$$
{\cal T}\!\left(\alpha_{0}\right)
   =(1-\lambda_{1})^{-1/2}
   =\Bigl(1-\tfrac12\Bigr)^{-1/2}=\sqrt2,
$$

i.e. with the usual mechanical normalisation

$$
T_{\rm phys}\!\left(\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}\right)
   =T_{\rm phys}\!\left(\tfrac12\right)
   =\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-\lambda_{1}}}
   =\frac{2\pi}{\omega_{1}}=2\pi\sqrt2,
$$

the constant harmonic period of $H_{4}=\tfrac12p^{2}+\tfrac14q^{2}$.
Stripping the inessential $2\pi$ factor this is the constant
normalised hypergeometric value ${\cal T}(1/2)=\sqrt2$, $ {\cal T}\equiv
(1-\alpha)^{-1/2}$ on the $m=2$ branch, viz. $T_{0}(1/2)=T_{0}(0)$,
which in the $\pi/\sin\pi\alpha$ convention is the constant
$\pi$.  The degenerate formal pair $n_{1}^{f}=2,n_{2}^{f}=4$,
$\alpha^{f}=1/4$, gives the ordinary harmonic normalisation
${\cal T}\equiv1$, $T_{\rm phys}\equiv2\pi$.  This is the $4,6$,
$\alpha_{0}=1/2$, constant period branch. ∎

4.text:
The $+$-eigenspace of $q\mapsto -q$ on
${\cal C}_{E}:y^{2}=2E-q^{2}+q^{n}$ is

$$
u_{r}(2m)=m-1=\frac n2-1,\qquad u_{r}(2m+1)=2m=n-1 ,
$$

so that $u_{r}(n)=n/2-1$ is the generic even value and
$u_{r}(n\pm1)=n\pm1-1$ is the generic odd value on the two
neighbours.  Apart from the degenerate $n=2$ limit the first non
trivial even member is

$$
n_{1}=4,\qquad n_{2}=6,\qquad m_{1}=\frac{n_{1}}2=2 ,
$$

and in general $n_{k}=2k+2$.  With the usual labelling

$$
\alpha_{0}:=\frac{n_{1}-1}{n_{2}}=\frac{3}{6}=\frac12 ,
$$

and

$$
\lambda_{0}
   =\frac{2}{n_{1}}\sqrt{\frac{n_{2}-n_{1}}{\,n_{1}/2\,}}
   =\frac{2}{4}\sqrt{\frac{2}{2}}=\frac12 ,
$$

the reduced Hamiltonian on the $+$ eigenspace is

$$
H_{n_{1}}(p,q)=\frac12\Bigl(p^{2}+q^{2}-\lambda_{0}q^{m_{1}}\Bigr)
